messages.content: How can I apply Evolutionary Algorithm in game Artificial Intelligence?

function.name: evolve_creatures
function.description: Apply the Evolutionary Algorithm to improve the creatures in a simulation over generations. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

population_size.description: The initial size of the creature population.

mutation_rate.description: The probability of mutation in each generation. This is a float type value.

generations.description: The number of generations to run the simulation.

fitness_goal.description: The fitness goal that the creatures should strive for. This is an optional parameter. Default: 1

message.content:
Below is a practical “recipe” you can follow if you’d like to start experimenting with evolutionary algorithms (EAs) inside your own game‑AI project – whether it’s a small prototype written in pure Python, a Unity / C# side‑project, or even a full‑blown Unreal Engine build. I’ll walk through the core concepts first, then give you a concrete **Python** skeleton that uses the helper function you posted (`evolve_creatures`). Finally, I’ll explain how you can hook this up to whatever runtime/game framework you’re actually building. --- ## 1️⃣ Core Concepts You Need To Know | Concept | What It Means In A Game Context | |---------|--------------------------------| | **Genome / Chromosome** | A compact data structure that encodes all tunable aspects of a character or agent (movement speed, jump height, neural network weights, strategy tables, …). Think of it as a *DNA* string. | | **Phenotype** | The real world entity created from a genome – i.e. the actual NPC instance running in the game. | | **Fitness Function** | A numeric score that tells us how well a phenotype performed in the game. For example:
• Survival time
• Distance travelled
• Score achieved
• Number of enemies defeated
• Composite weighted sum of several objectives | | **Selection** | Picking genomes that did better so they get more chances to reproduce. Common methods: tournament selection, roulette wheel, rank‑based. | | **Crossover (Recombination)** | Mixing two parent genomes to create one or more offspring. Typical operators: single‑point, multi‑point, uniform crossover. | | **Mutation** | Randomly tweaking parts of a genome to keep diversity alive. Usually applied at low rates per gene. | | **Population Size & Generational Loop** | How many agents exist simultaneously and how long you let them play before moving onto the next generation. | ### Why EAs Are Useful In Games | Benefit | Example | |--------|----------| | Handles complex, non‑linear search spaces where gradients don’t exist | Tuning a deep RL policy without backpropagation | | Naturally supports multiple conflicting goals | Balancing aggression vs stealth | | Works well when evaluation cost is high but parallelizable | Running thousands of simulated battles offline | | Produces diverse solutions that may inspire designers | Discovering novel movement patterns or tactics | --- ## 2️⃣ High‑Level Workflow Diagram ``` ┌───────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ │ Generate Initial Gen │◄──► Create Phenotypes │ ├───────────────────────┤ └──────▲────────────┘ │ Evaluate Fitness │ │ ├───────────────────────┤ ▼ │ Select Parents │ ┌───────────────────────┐ ├───────────────────────┼──▶ │ Recombine + Mutate │ │ Produce Offspring │ ├───────────────────────┤ ├───────────────────────┴──▶ │ Replace Population │ │ Next Generation │ └───────────────────────┘ └───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘ │ ▲ Repeat Until Goal Met │ │ │ End Simulation │ ``` --- ## 3️⃣ Concrete Python Skeleton Using Your Helper Tool ```python from typing import List, Dict, Any import random import math # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 1. Genome Representation ------------------------------------------------- # ------------------------------------------------------------------ class CreatureGenome: """ Simple genome holding three traits: - move_speed : [0.1 , 10] - jump_height: [0.1 , 20] - aggressiveness: [0 , 1] (probability of attacking) """ def __init__(self, genes=None): # Genes stored as dictionary for readability self.genes = genes or { "move_speed": random.uniform(0.1, 10), "jump_height": random.uniform(0.1, 20), "aggressiveness": random.random() } def mutate(self, rate=0.02): """Apply Gaussian noise to each gene based on mutation rate.""" for key in self.genes.keys(): if random.random() < rate: old_val = self.genes[key] perturbation = random.gauss(0, 0.1 * abs(old_val)) new_val = old_val + perturbation # Clamp values to sensible ranges if key == "move_speed": new_val = min(max(new_val, 0.1), 10) elif key == "jump_height": new_val = min(max(new_val, 0.1), 20) else: # aggressiveness new_val = min(max(new_val, 0.0), 1.0) self.genes[key] = new_val @staticmethod def crossover(parent_a, parent_b): """Uniform crossover between two parents.""" child_genes = {} for k in parent_a.genes: child_genes[k] = parent_a.genes[k] if random.random() < 0.5 \ else parent_b.genes[k] return CreatureGenome(child_genes) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 2. Simulated Environment --------------------------------------------- # ------------------------------------------------------------------ def simulate_game(genome: CreatureGenome) -> float: """ Dummy simulator that returns a fitness score. In practice replace this with calls to your game engine! """ ms = genome.genes["move_speed"] jh = genome.genes["jump_height"] aggr = genome.genes["aggressiveness"] # Very naive scoring formula just for illustration distance_travelled = ms * 30 # faster means farther jumps_successful = int(jh > 8) * 15 # good jump height gives bonus attack_bonus = aggr * 25 # higher aggressiveness yields points total_score = distance_travelled + jumps_successful + attack_bonus return total_score # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3. Evolutionary Loop ----------------------------------------------- # ------------------------------------------------------------------ def run_evolution(population_size: int, mutation_rate: float, generations: int, fitness_goal: float = 200): # --- Initialise population --- population: List[CreatureGenome] = [ CreatureGenome() for _ in range(population_size) ] best_fitness_overall = -math.inf best_individual = None for gen_idx in range(generations): print(f"\n=== Generation {gen_idx+1}/{generations} ===") # ---- Evaluation Phase ---- fitness_scores = [] for idx, individual in enumerate(population): fit = simulate_game(individual) fitness_scores.append((fit, individual)) if fit > best_fitness_overall: best_fitness_overall = fit best_individual = individual # Sort descending by fitness fitness_scores.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) top_10_percent_index = max(int(len(population)*0.1)-1, 0) elite_count = len(population)//10 elites = [indiv for _, indiv in fitness_scores[:elite_count]] print(f"Top fitness this gen: {fitness_scores[0][0]:.2f}") print(f"Best overall so far: {best_fitness_overall:.2f}") # Check termination condition if best_fitness_overall >= fitness_goal: print("\n✅ FITNESS GOAL ACHIEVED!") break # ---- Breeding Phase ---- new_population = [] while len(new_population) < population_size: # Tournament selection among elites parent_a = random.choice(elites) parent_b = random.choice(elites) child = CreatureGenome.crossover(parent_a, parent_b) child.mutate(rate=mutation_rate) new_population.append(child) population = new_population # Return the best found genome return best_individual, best_fitness_overall # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 4. Hook Into Provided Helper Function ------------------------------ # ------------------------------------------------------------------ if __name__ == "__main__": # Call the helper you supplied result = functions.evolve_creatures({ "population_size": 120, "mutation_rate": 0.03, "generations": 60, "fitness_goal": 250 }) # The helper itself would internally do something similar to above. # If you prefer to see our custom implementation instead: best_genome, best_fit = run_evolution( population_size=120, mutation_rate=0.03, generations=60, fitness_goal=250 ) print("\n--- Final Best Individual ---") print(best_genome.genes) print("Final fitness:", best_fit) ``` ### What Happens Here? 1. **Genomes** encode three simple attributes. 2. **`simulate_game()`** pretends to run a battle/simulation and spits out a scalar reward. 3. **Evolutionary loop** evaluates everyone, keeps the top % (“elites”), breeds new individuals via crossover/mutation, repeats. 4. When the target fitness is hit or generations finish, the algorithm stops. Feel free to swap out the dummy simulator with a real API call to your game engine—just make sure the fitness function runs fast enough because it gets called millions of times during training! --- ## 4️⃣ Integrating With Real Game Engines | Platform | Integration Strategy | Tips | |-----------|----------------------|------| | **Unity (C#/MonoBehaviour)** | • Run evolution off‑line in a separate process.
• Export best genomes as JSON/text files.
• Import those files into Unity and instantiate prefabs configured by the genome. | Keep the simulation lightweight; consider using Unity's Job System or Burst compiler for massive parallelism. | | **Unreal (Blueprints/C++)** | • Write a CLI utility in C++ that reads/writes CSV/JSON.
- Or embed a tiny Python interpreter (via pybind11) directly in UE. | Leverage UE’s built‑in physics and pathfinding for realistic evaluations. | | **Godot (GDScript/Python)** | • Godot now has experimental Python support!
• Alternatively, write a GDScript wrapper around the same logic. | Godot’s scene system makes spawning/destroying entities trivial. | | **Custom Browser/Game (JavaScript/WebGL)** | • Port the GA logic to JavaScript (or WebAssembly).
• Store genomes in localStorage or IndexedDB. | Use requestAnimationFrame loops to evaluate fitness incrementally. | ### Parallelizing Evaluations If evaluating a single genome takes seconds, you’ll quickly hit bottlenecks. Two common tricks: 1. **Simulate Multiple Worlds Concurrently** – spawn N independent instances of the game (headless mode) and distribute genomes across them. 2. **Vectorized Simulation** – design your game logic such that you can batch update many agents in a single tick (common in grid‑world or RTS simulations). Both approaches reduce wall‑clock time dramatically and allow larger populations/generations. --- ## 5️⃣ Quick Checklist Before You Start ☑️ Decide on **what you want to optimize** (score, survival, style). ☑️ Design a **compact yet expressive genome**. ☑️ Build a **fast, deterministic evaluator** that maps a genome → fitness. ☑️ Pick suitable **selection/crossover/mutation** hyperparameters. ☑️ Test on a **small toy problem** first (maybe a 2D platformer level). ☑️ Scale up gradually once you confirm correctness. Once you’ve got a working pipeline, you can experiment with advanced techniques: - **Neuroevolution** (tune NN weights directly). - **Cooperative co‑evolution** (multiple species evolving together). - **Dynamic fitness shaping** (gradually increase difficulty). - **Hybridization** (EA + reinforcement learning). Happy hacking—and remember: the beauty of evolutionary computation lies not only in finding optimal solutions but also in discovering unexpected strategies that human designers rarely think of!
